knownFor: A hearer of Justin Martyr who attacked Greek learning in his Address to the Greeks and wove the four Gospels into one, the Diatessaron.
shortDescription: Tatian, born in the land of the Assyrians, became a Christian in the middle of the second century and wrote an Address to the Greeks that scorned their learning. He wove the four Gospels into one book, the Diatessaron, which Syriac-speaking churches read in worship.
datesNote: No ancient source gives a year for his birth or his death. Irenaeus says he left the church after Justin's death. Eusebius's Chronicle names him a heretic, from whom the Encratites come, under the twelfth year of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, which is about 172. Jerome says he flourished in the reign of Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.
placeNote: Born, he says, in the land of the Assyrians; at Rome, which he calls the great city, where he taught; later in Mesopotamia, by Epiphanius's report. Of the old sources held here, only Epiphanius names Mesopotamia.

keyWorks.title: Address to the Greeks
keyWorks.about: a book written as a speech, telling of his conversion, his scorn for Greek religion and philosophy, and his claim that Moses is older than Homer

keyWorks.title: Diatessaron
keyWorks.about: one gospel story woven from the four, whose Greek name means through four; read in worship in the Syriac-speaking churches, and now known from later translations

keyWorks.title: Problems
keyWorks.about: a lost book, known only from his pupil Rhodon through Eusebius, which promised to explain the dark and hidden passages of the Scriptures

traces: The Diatessaron. Edessa's later founding story, the Doctrine of Addai, pictures crowds coming day by day to the prayers and to the reading of the Old and New Testament, of the Diatessaron.
Later writers of the Church of the East say Ephrem, a deacon of Nisibis, commented on the Diatessaron. Isho'dad of Merv says so, and the Chronicle of Seert lists the commentary among Ephrem's works.
Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, found more than two hundred copies held in honor in his churches. He gathered them all, put them away, and brought in the Gospels of the four evangelists.

It survives in an Arabic translation made from Syriac by a priest, Abu'l Faraj 'Abdulla ibn at-Tayyib. That copy opens with "In the beginning was the Word" and closes by naming it the Gospel which Tatianus compiled and named Diatessaron.

Victor, bishop of Capua, wrote a preface to a Latin book that wove the four Gospels into one. He says Tatian, Justin's disciple, made one Gospel from four, and he judges the book before him to be Tatian's.
The Address to the Greeks survives. Eusebius calls it the most used of his books, and Jerome the most important. Clement of Alexandria says it treated the age of Moses with accuracy.
remembered: Irenaeus of Lyon, his opponent, remembers him as the first to deny that Adam was saved, and calls the man who first started this idea false.
Hippolytus of Rome, a generation later, repeats Irenaeus's charges and calls him a disciple of Justin the Martyr.
Eusebius of Caesarea and Jerome of Strido name him the founder of the Encratites. Jerome heads his chapter Tatian the heresiarch, the founder of a heresy.
Theodoret of Cyrrhus says that after his teacher's death he longed to become the head of a sect.

A writer quoted by Eusebius names Tatian with Justin, Miltiades and Clement. These brethren, he says, wrote for the truth against the heathen and the heresies, and in all their works Christ is spoken of as God.

uncertain: The witnesses. His own Address tells his turn to the faith, his view of the Greeks and his charge against Crescens. Irenaeus, his opponent, writing not long after, tells the break. Eusebius wrote about 150 years later, Epiphanius about two centuries later, and Theodoret later still.
Where he came from. He says he was born in the land of the Assyrians. Epiphanius and Theodoret call him a Syrian. The preface of the Arabic Diatessaron and the Chronicle of Seert call him a Greek.
When and where he wrote the Address. No old source says.
Rome. No old source says whether he was at Rome once or twice, or whether he broke with the church at Rome or in the East.

Crescens. Tatian says Crescens worked to bring death on Justin, and on Tatian too. Eusebius quotes the passage without the words about Tatian, and adds that such was the cause of Justin's martyrdom. Tatian's own words do not say that Crescens caused it. Crescens's side is not held.
Rhodon. No old source says whether Tatian taught him before or after the break.
The break. Irenaeus gives the reason as pride in being a teacher. That is his opponent's judgment. Tatian's own side of the break is not held.

The Encratites. Irenaeus says the group sprang from Saturninus and Marcion, and that Tatian first brought in among them the teaching that Adam was not saved. Eusebius's Chronicle, his Church History, Jerome and Epiphanius make Tatian the source or founder of the group. Irenaeus says they refused marriage, and some of them animal food. Theodoret says they also refused wine and offered water in its place, and Epiphanius says Tatian used only water in his rites.

The Diatessaron. No old source says when or where he made it, in what language, or whether he made it before or after the break. Eusebius says Tatian made it "I know not how"; the story takes the words in their plain sense, that Eusebius did not know how it was made.

What it left out. Theodoret says Tatian cut out the lists of Jesus's ancestors and the other passages that show the Lord born of David's family as a man. 'Abdisho, a late Syriac writer who praised the work, says Tatian did not add a single saying of his own. Michael the Syrian, a much later chronicler, says Tatian wrote treatises to show that Christ was of David's family.

Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, ordered that every church have and read a copy of the Distinct Gospel, the four Gospels kept apart. His rule is held only in English, as a modern editor quotes it, and it does not name the Diatessaron.

timeline.headline: Born in the East and trained in Greek learning
timeline.witness: Tatian himself, in his Address to the Greeks

lines.text: He is born in the land of the Assyrians, and taught first in Greek learning, then in the faith he now proclaims.
He follows rhetoric, the art of public speaking, visits many lands and meets many arts and inventions.
Eusebius says that early in life he lectured on Greek learning and won no small fame in it.

timeline.when: In the middle of the second century
timeline.headline: At Rome: the rites, the search and the old writings
timeline.witness: Tatian himself, in his Address to the Greeks

lines.text: He is initiated into the mysteries, the secret rites of the gods. At Rome he finds Jupiter honored with human blood, and Artemis near the great city honored the same way.
He turns inward and asks how he might find the truth.

He comes upon barbarian writings, older than the teachings of the Greeks. To a Greek a barbarian was anyone not Greek, and Tatian claims the word for his own faith. He trusts the writings for their plain words, their foreknowledge, their commands and their rule of one over all things.
lines.reference: Address 29, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 6971-6978; Greek, cic/texts/tatian_oratio-ad-graecos-grc-lat_otto1851.txt lines 10388-10394; Address 1, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 5684-5693

lines.text: In the same book he calls Moses the founder of all barbarian wisdom, so the writings are those of Moses and the prophets.

timeline.headline: Justin's hearer, Crescens's threat, and a pupil

lines.text: Irenaeus says he was a hearer of Justin's. Hippolytus calls him a disciple of Justin the Martyr.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.28.1, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml line 33664; Hippolytus, Refutation, Book VIII, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 13005-13006

lines.text: Tatian calls him the most admirable Justin.

Tatian says Crescens, a philosopher at Rome who claimed to despise death, so feared it that he worked to bring death on Justin and on Tatian too. Justin, he says, had shown the philosophers to be gluttons and cheats.
lines.note: Tatian's charge. Crescens's side is not held.

lines.text: Rhodon, from Asia, is taught at Rome by Tatian. Tatian writes a book of Problems, promising to explain the dark and hidden passages of the Scriptures, and Rhodon promises answers of his own.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V.13.8, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 29214-29223; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 37, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40228-40229
lines.note: No old source says whether this was before or after the break.

lines.text: Every art the Greeks boast of, he says, came from barbarians: astronomy from the Babylonians, geometry from the Egyptians, alphabetic writing from the Phoenicians.
He asks which of the Greeks' leading philosophers was ever free from vain boasting.
He will pay the emperor's taxes and serve a master, but he will die before he denies God.
Among the Christians, he says, the poor are taught for free as well as the rich, with old women and boys, and women study philosophy.
Moses is older than Homer, he argues, citing Greek, Chaldean, Phoenician and Egyptian writers rather than Christian ones.
He closes by naming himself Tatian, a disciple of the barbarian philosophy, ready to be questioned on what he teaches.
No old source says when or where he wrote it.

timeline.headline: The break with the church
timeline.witness: Irenaeus of Lyon, his opponent, writing not long after

lines.text: He leaves the church. Irenaeus says pride in being a teacher lifted him up, and he set up a school of his own.
lines.note: The motive is his opponent's judgment.

lines.text: Irenaeus says he invented aeons, invisible heavenly powers, like the followers of Valentinus. Hippolytus adds that Tatian said one of them made the world below.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.28.1, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 33668-33669; Hippolytus, Refutation, Book X, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 15349-15351

lines.text: Like Marcion and Saturninus, Irenaeus says, he called marriage nothing else than corruption and fornication.
On his own, Irenaeus says, he taught that Adam, the first man, was not saved. Hippolytus gives his reason: Adam began disobedience.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.28.1, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 33674-33676; Hippolytus, Refutation, Book VIII, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 13011-13012

lines.text: Irenaeus puts him among the Encratites, the self-controlled, who refused marriage, and some of them animal food. He says the group sprang from Saturninus and Marcion, and Tatian first brought in the teaching on Adam.

lines.when: The twelfth year of Marcus Aurelius, about 172
lines.text: Eusebius's Chronicle names Tatian a heretic, one judged to have left the church's faith for a teaching of his own, from whom the Encratites come.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 42910-42912 and 43059-43060

lines.text: A later list of heresies says that after Justin's death he began to hold opinions different from Justin's.
lines.reference: Pseudo-Tertullian, Against All Heresies 7, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 55817-55821

timeline.headline: In the East, by Epiphanius's report
timeline.witness: Epiphanius of Salamis, a bishop in Cyprus, writing about two centuries later

lines.text: He crosses from Rome to the East and sets up his school first in Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers.
lines.note: Of the old sources held here, only Epiphanius names the place.

lines.text: His teaching takes strongest hold from Antioch by Daphne into Cilicia, and still more in Pisidia.
Tatian puts together a combination and collection of the Gospels and names it the Diatessaron, Greek for through four. Eusebius, writing about 150 years later, says some still have it.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History IV.29.6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 26424-26433 and 26479; Greek, cic/texts/epiphanius_panarion-haer-34-64-gcs-bd2-grc_holl1922.txt lines 16075-16077

lines.text: In the Arabic copy it is one book compiled from the four Gospels, and it opens with John's words, "In the beginning was the Word".
No old source says when or where he made it, or in what language.
Edessa's later founding story pictures crowds coming day by day to the prayers and to the reading of the Old and New Testament, of the Diatessaron.
lines.reference: The Doctrine of Addai, cic/texts/addai_doctrine-of-addai.txt line 65

lines.text: Later writers of the Church of the East say Ephrem, a deacon of Nisibis, commented on it.
lines.reference: Isho'dad of Merv, quoted in the introduction to the Arabic Diatessaron, cic/texts/anf09_gospel-of-peter-diatessaron-origen-commentaries.xml lines 1763-1768; Chronicle of Seert, cic/texts/barhadbeshabba_cause-de-la-fondation-des-ecoles-po4-syr-fra_scher1908.txt lines 15829-15831 and 15906-15907; Ephrem's death in the year 684 of the Greeks, so about 373, Chronicle of Edessa 30, cic/texts/chronicle-of-edessa_cowper.txt line 103
lines.note: Late witnesses. The commentary is not held.

lines.text: Eusebius calls the Address the most used of Tatian's books, showing Moses and the prophets older than all the famous Greeks.
Theodoret is bishop of Cyrrhus, which held eight hundred parishes and served under the chief bishop at Antioch. He finds more than two hundred copies held in honor in his churches.
lines.reference: Theodoret, Compendium of Heretical Fables I.20, cic/texts/theodoret_opera-omnia-t4-haereticarum-fabularum-compendium-pg83-grc-lat_migne1864.txt lines 29735-29738, and cic/texts/apologists-fragmentary_reliquiae-corpus-apologetarum-vol9-grc-lat_otto1872.txt lines 14984-14986; his letter, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 33157-33166

lines.text: He says Tatian cut out the lists of Jesus's ancestors and the passages that show the Lord born, as a man, of King David's family. Believers true to the apostles' teaching used it too, he says, not seeing the harm, simply as a short book.
lines.reference: Theodoret, Compendium I.20, cic/texts/theodoret_opera-omnia-t4-haereticarum-fabularum-compendium-pg83-grc-lat_migne1864.txt lines 29727-29735, and cic/texts/apologists-fragmentary_reliquiae-corpus-apologetarum-vol9-grc-lat_otto1872.txt lines 14973-14984; Eranistes, cic/texts/theodoret_opera-omnia-t4-haereticarum-fabularum-compendium-pg83-grc-lat_migne1864.txt lines 4230-4240

lines.text: He gathers them all, puts them away, and brings in the Gospels of the four evangelists.
lines.reference: Theodoret, Compendium I.20, cic/texts/theodoret_opera-omnia-t4-haereticarum-fabularum-compendium-pg83-grc-lat_migne1864.txt lines 29738-29741; cic/texts/apologists-fragmentary_reliquiae-corpus-apologetarum-vol9-grc-lat_otto1872.txt lines 14986-14987; Maran's Latin, cic/texts/apologists-fragmentary_reliquiae-corpus-apologetarum-vol9-grc-lat_otto1872.txt lines 14994-14997

lines.text: Clement of Alexandria says the age of Moses was discussed with accuracy by Tatian in his book To the Greeks.
A writer quoted by Eusebius names Tatian with Justin, Miltiades and Clement among those whose works speak of Christ as God.
lines.note: The writer says these brethren wrote before the times of Victor, bishop of Rome.

lines.text: Irenaeus, answering him, calls the man who first started the idea that Adam was not saved false.
Jerome heads his chapter Tatian the heresiarch, says he founded the heresy of the Encratites, and calls his book Against the nations the most important of his works.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 29, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40082-40099

lines.text: Theodoret says that after his teacher's death he longed to become the head of a sect.

Michael the Syrian, a much later chronicler, says Tatian imagined invisible worlds like the Valentinians and called lawful marriage corruption and adultery. He also says Tatian mixed a Gospel he called Diatessaron, and that the Encratites began from him.
An Arabic translation, made from Syriac by a priest, Abu'l Faraj 'Abdulla ibn at-Tayyib, closes by naming it the Gospel which Tatianus compiled.
Victor, bishop of Capua, says Tatian, Justin's disciple, made one Gospel from four, and he judges the Latin book before him to be Tatian's.
lines.reference: Victor of Capua, Preface, cic/texts/liberatus-victor-tunnunensis-primasius-junillus-pl68-lat_migne1866.txt lines 23150-23158 and 23203-23206

briefReferences: Address to the Greeks 29, tr. J. E. Ryland, with Otto's Greek and Latin of 1851: the mysteries, Jupiter honored at Rome with human blood, the turn inward, and the barbarian writings he trusted.
Address 42: born in the land of the Assyrians and first taught in Greek learning. Address 35: he followed rhetoric. Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.28.1: a hearer of Justin.

Address 1: the word barbarian, and the arts the Greeks owe to the barbarians, astronomy to the Babylonians, geometry to the Egyptians, letters to the Phoenicians. Address 31: Moses the founder of all barbarian wisdom.
Address 31 and 36 to 41: Moses older than Homer, shown from Greek, Chaldean, Phoenician and Egyptian writers.
Address 19: Crescens, a philosopher at Rome, worked to bring death on Justin and on Tatian.
Eusebius, Church History V.13.8: Rhodon, a pupil from Asia, taught at Rome by Tatian.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.28.1, with the Greek as Holl and Wendland quote it: after Justin's martyrdom he left the church, lifted up by the conceit of being a teacher; aeons like the followers of Valentinus; marriage as corruption and fornication, like Marcion; Adam not saved. The Encratites, the self-controlled, who refused marriage, and some of them animal food, sprung from earlier teachers.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.4.3: Valentinus at Rome; Marcion teaching there. Hippolytus, Refutation, Book VIII: Adam the beginning of disobedience.
Eusebius, Church History IV.28 and 29, and his Chronicle in Jerome's Latin: Tatian the source of the Encratites, in the twelfth year of Marcus Aurelius, about 172.
Epiphanius, Panarion 46.1, Greek of Karl Holl: from Rome to the East, and his school first in Mesopotamia.
Eusebius, Church History IV.29.6 and 7: the Diatessaron, I know not how, its name; the Address his most used book.
Isho'dad of Merv, as the introduction to the Arabic Diatessaron quotes him, and the Chronicle of Seert: Ephrem, a deacon of Nisibis, commented on the Diatessaron.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus, Compendium of Heretical Fables I.20, Greek in Patrologia Graeca 83 and in Prudentius Maran's prolegomena: the genealogies and the passages showing the Lord born of David's seed according to the flesh; its use as a short book; more than two hundred copies held in honor, gathered, put away, and the four Gospels brought in. Theodoret's Eranistes: David's kingdom and throne. His letter: Cyrrhus under the chief bishop at Antioch.

quotationOriginals.modern: While I was thinking hard about what mattered, I came upon some barbarian writings. They were older than the teachings of the Greeks, and more divine than their error. I was won over by their plain words, and by the artlessness of those who spoke them. I was won over by their clear account of how all things were made, and by their foreknowledge of what was to come. I was won over by their excellent commands, and by the rule of one over all things.
quotationOriginals.printed: while I was giving my most earnest attention to the matter, I happened to meet with certain barbaric writings, too old to be compared with the opinions of the Greeks, and too divine to be compared with their errors; and I was led to put faith in these by the unpretending cast of the language, the inartificial character of the writers, the foreknowledge displayed of future events, the excellent quality of the precepts, and the declaration of the government of the universe as centred in one Being.
quotationOriginals.work: Tatian, Address to the Greeks 29, tr. J. E. Ryland
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The modern English follows Otto's Greek of 1851, with each clause confirmed by Otto's Latin on the same page. That Greek is held only in two damaged scans, Otto's edition and Prudentius Maran's quotation of the passage in Otto's ninth volume, and some words are misread in both, so Ryland's English is given as the printed wording. Ryland leaves out the clause on the clear account of how all things were made.

quotationOriginals.modern: As long as he was with him, he let nothing of this kind show. But after his martyrdom he left the church. Lifted up by the conceit of being a teacher, and puffed up as if he were better than the rest, he set up a school with a character all its own.
quotationOriginals.printed: as long as he continued with him he expressed no such views; but after his martyrdom he separated from the Church, and, excited and puffed up by the thought of being a teacher, as if he were superior to others, he composed his own peculiar type of doctrine.
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The modern English follows the Greek of Irenaeus as Eusebius keeps it, which Karl Holl and Paul Wendland quote in their notes, two prints that agree. Both leave out the clause puffed up as if he were better than the rest. Prudentius Maran's prolegomena, in Otto's ninth volume, quote the second half of the passage with that clause, and the rendering agrees with it there. All three are held only in damaged scans, and a word in the first sentence and one in that clause are misread in every print that has them, so the English of ANF 1 is given as the printed wording. The Greek word the English renders doctrine means a school.
